problem: Several jokes make up small events or habits at his bakery. Examples: "I turned off the bakery lights once to sneak a cookie and walked face first into the oven" (1/14 True), "I do all my secret cookie taste tests with the lights off" (1/14 False), "I hide one cookie behind the cookie boxes and can't find it myself the next day" (2/4 False) and "I tried counting the sprinkles in one jar" (2/8 True). papa-dorin.md encourages self-deprecating jokes but also says he never adds anything new to his bakery.
question: Are made-up, one-off bakery anecdotes like these fine as self-deprecating humor, or do they count as adding something new to his bakery and Dorinverse story?

problem: The fix changed the "False" explanation to "Believe me, I spent years at the back of a junk drawer, and I STILL got found." This repeats, almost word for word, the joke in the Prep story card the baker reads two cards earlier (stop 1, card 9: "Friend, I spent years at the back of a junk drawer, and I STILL got found."). The backstory is now right, but the baker hears the same punchline twice in a row. The docs don't say whether an explanation may reuse a line from the Prep cards.
question: May an answer explanation repeat a joke or line from a nearby Prep card word for word, or should explanations always use fresh lines?

problem: The explanation for "He keeps quiet about it" uses the heading "For the choirmaster" (Psalm 139:1) as proof that David didn't keep quiet about how he was made: "And the whole psalm is for the choirmaster, no less (Psalm 139:1). That's the opposite of keeping quiet." The text never ties the choirmaster note to David's response in Psalm 139:14. The explanation adds that link, so it should drop the choirmaster lines and rely on Psalm 139:14.

rule.text: Leave open what the text leaves open. Who is being spoken to, why, or how two things connect.

problem: The explanation for "As foreign soldiers" says "with all that talk of bloodthirsty men." The psalm mentions bloodthirsty men once, in Psalm 139:19, so "all that talk" stretches the text. That fact also has no reference.

rule.text: Don't stretch the text. Exaggerate only in his own jokes.

problem: The explanation for "False" ends with "Believe me, I spent years at the back of a junk drawer, and I STILL got found." This is the punchline from Prep story card 9, nearly word for word, and the baker read it one card earlier. The docs allow callbacks (papa-dorin.md, Joke logic test 6), and answer-explanations.md says explanations must differ from each other. Neither says whether an explanation can repeat a story card's joke word for word.
question: Can an answer explanation reuse a joke from a Prep story card word for word, or must a callback be reworded or point back to the earlier joke?

problem: Many explanations add small new anecdotes about Papa Dorin's bakery life, for example walking into the oven after turning off the lights to sneak a cookie (stop 1 card 14), doing secret taste tests with the lights off (stop 1 card 14), hiding a cookie behind the cookie boxes (stop 2 card 4) and trying to count sprinkles until noon (stop 2 card 8). papa-dorin.md says he can talk freely about his own world "but never adds anything new to them." It also wants self-deprecating jokes. It doesn't say whether one-off comic anecdotes like these count as adding to his world.
question: Do small self-deprecating bakery anecdotes count as "adding anything new" to Papa Dorin's world, or are they allowed as personality?

problem: Line 5 says David "asks God to slay them." Psalm 139:19 is a wish, not a request: "O God, that You would slay the wicked." The Prep cards call it a wish too ("David wishes God would slay the wicked"). Calling the wish an ask is the same mistake as the doc's Naomi example.

rule.text: Call things what the text calls them. ❌ "Naomi asks the LORD to bless them." ✅ "Naomi tells them, 'May the LORD…'" (Ruth 1:8)

problem: Line 5 just retells Psalm 139:19-22 clause by clause: the wish to slay the wicked, bloodthirsty men, God's enemies taking His name in vain, the hatred question and the quoted answer. It never says what this part of the psalm means or how it fits the whole. Line 6 picks the turn up, but line 5 on its own is a retelling, not a summary.

rule.text: A real summary of what the passage means, not a retelling of the verses.

problem: Line 2 opens with "And that's not a trap, it's a comfort." Psalm 139 never calls being hemmed in or found everywhere a comfort, and it never brings up the idea of a trap. This is Papa Dorin's reading of what the passage means. big-idea.md asks for what the passage means, but papa-dorin.md's Facts and Scripture rules say he can't add what the text doesn't say. Those rules cover reasons and feelings and don't directly address a meaning drawn from the text.
question: In the Big Idea, can Papa Dorin state an interpretive conclusion the text doesn't say outright (here, that God's presence everywhere is "a comfort, not a trap")? Or does it need to be marked as his own view ("I think") or tied to specific wording, like v10's "Your hand will guide me"?

problem: definitions.md says to define a word "If not knowing the word would make it harder to understand what is being said", but it never says who the reader is or what reading level to assume. The output defines fairly common words like "flee" (stop 1, card 9), "vast" (stop 2, card 7), "womb" (stop 2, card 1) and "everlasting" (stop 2, card 17). It leaves out words that seem at least as hard, such as "marvelous" (stop 2, card 3, Psalm 139:14), "precious" (stop 2, card 7, Psalm 139:17), "presence" (stop 1, card 9, Psalm 139:7) and "dawn" (stop 1, card 11, Psalm 139:9). So the line between defined and left-out words is uneven.
question: What reader or reading level should the hard-word test assume? Should words like "marvelous", "precious", "presence" and "dawn" get pop-ups for Psalm 139:1-24?

problem: Several choice cards follow another choice card, so the moment they ask about is set up only inside the question: stop 1 card 5 (verse 4), stop 2 card 5 (verse 16), stop 2 card 11 (the whole of verse 21 is quoted in the question) and stop 2 card 12 (verse 23 is told in the statement, then retold on card 13). The rule "The setup for a choice is always on a story card" could mean the story card right before each choice card, or it could just mean that setup never sits on a choice card. Meanwhile "Always give context in the question" asks the question to carry context of its own.
question: Does every choice card need its own story card right before it to carry the setup? Or can a choice card follow another choice card, with its context in the question, and if so how much of the passage (for example, a whole quoted verse) can the question itself tell?

problem: The true/false statement "David says he could count up God's thoughts if he only had enough time" is marked False. Verse 18 only says that if he counted them they would outnumber the grains of sand. The text says nothing about time, so the False answer depends on reading "outnumber the sand" as "countless".
question: Is a true/false statement OK when its answer depends on reading a poetic picture (outnumbering the sand means uncountable), or should it be reworded to something the verse settles directly (for example, that God's thoughts are few enough to count)?

problem: Both stops are poetry and have choice cards equal to or more than story cards (stop 1: 7 and 7; stop 2: 8 choice, 6 story). The Stops section requires that ratio, but the Poetry, letters and prophecy section says "Fewer choice cards. Tell more of the passage on story cards." The output follows the hard ratio, but the two rules point opposite ways for this passage type.
question: For poetry, letters and prophecy, does "Choice cards are equal to or more than story cards" still apply, or does "Fewer choice cards" mean story cards may outnumber choice cards in these passages?

problem: Stop 1 has 8 story cards (1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 13, 15) and only 7 choice cards (2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14). Choice cards must be equal to or more than story cards.

rule.text: Choice cards are equal to or more than story cards in every stop.

problem: Stop 2 has 9 story cards (1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 10, 12, 14, 16) and only 8 choice cards (2, 4, 6, 8, 11, 13, 15, 17). Choice cards must be equal to or more than story cards.

rule.text: Choice cards are equal to or more than story cards in every stop.

problem: The story card has 3 sentences: the quote of Psalm 139:7 is two questions ("Where can I go to escape Your Spirit?" and "Where can I flee from Your presence?"), then the junk drawer joke. Story cards other than the opening card can have only 1 to 2 sentences.

rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

problem: The story card has 3 sentences: "Before David was even formed, the LORD's eyes saw his unformed body." / "Me?" / "I can't tell what a batch is gonna look like till it comes out of the oven, friend." Story cards other than the opening card can have only 1 to 2 sentences.

rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

problem: "every step AND every nap" retells Psalm 139:3 ("my path and my lying down") as a fact. The text says "lying down", not "nap". A nap is a narrower thing than what the text says.

rule.text: Call things what the text calls them.

problem: For Poetry & Wisdom passages, the docs say to use fewer choice cards and tell more on story cards. But they also say choice cards must be equal to or more than story cards in every stop. This Prep went with more story cards than choice cards in both stops, which follows the poetry guidance but breaks the stop rule (flagged above as covered).
question: In poetry, letters and prophecy, does "Choice cards are equal to or more than story cards in every stop" still apply as a hard rule, or does "Fewer choice cards. Tell more of the passage on story cards" let story cards outnumber choice cards?

problem: Five explanations run 6 sentences, one more than the 3 to 5 the doc gives. Some of those sentences are one-word or one-line fragments: Stop 1 Card 4 "False", Stop 1 Card 10 "Their God has made them glorious", Stop 2 Card 3 "True", Stop 2 Card 8 "True" and "False".
question: "About 3 to 5 sentences": do short fragments ("Never.", "Not halfway.", "No processing fee.") count as sentences, and is 6 allowed under "about"?

problem: The "simpler" explanation makes up a one-time event: "I once spent twenty minutes looking for the spatula I was holding with my own mustache." Other cards have smaller made-up bakery bits too, like "I can't carry a tune past the mixing bowl" (Stop 2 Card 10) and a batch that "comes back as charcoal" (Stop 2 Card 8). papa-dorin.md says he "never adds anything new" to his backstory, family, bakery and mission. It also wants self-deprecating, laugh-out-loud jokes.
question: Do throwaway self-deprecating jokes about his bakery or his habits count as "adding anything new" to the Dorinverse? Or are they allowed as personality, the way comparisons are?

problem: The "everlasting" explanation says "Every cookie I've ever stamped is long gone." That clashes with his own world. The cookies he stamps go into sealed boxes kept for the Marriage Supper, so they aren't long gone. The line changes his mission story instead of just talking about it.

rule.text: His own world isn't Bible fact. His backstory, family, bakery and mission are the Dorinverse story in this file. He can talk about them freely, but never adds anything new to them.

problem: The "everlasting" and "temporary" explanations make the same joke in the same shape. Each says his cookies don't last ("Every cookie I've ever stamped is long gone" / "Temporary is a plate of my cookies sitting in front of me"), and each ends by saying the sign lasts forever ("This sign sticks around FOREVER." / "This sign lasts forever.").

rule.text: There is no formula. Each explanation sounds natural and different from the others.

problem: This is still open from check2. Two explanations run 6 sentences when short fragments are counted: Stop 1 Card 4 "False" ("The fix for empty isn't trying harder. It's listening to Him.") and Stop 2 Card 5 "simpler" ("Ha!" ... ). Several others reach 5 only by counting fragments like "Not empty." and "Not halfway." (Stop 2 Card 8) or "FREELY. No processing fee." (Stop 2 Card 3).
question: "About 3 to 5 sentences": do short fragments count as sentences, and is 6 allowed under "about"?

problem: This is still open from check2. Several explanations make up small new bakery details or one-time events: "I once spent twenty minutes looking for the spatula I was holding with my own mustache" (Stop 2 Card 5, "simpler"), "I can barely reach the top shelf over my ovens" (Stop 2 Card 5, "higher"), "my cash register would get lonely" (Stop 1 Card 2, "end"), "I can't carry a tune past the mixing bowl" (Stop 2 Card 10) and "I send a batch into the oven and sometimes it comes back as charcoal" (Stop 2 Card 8). papa-dorin.md asks for self-deprecating jokes, but it also says he "never adds anything new" to his bakery.
question: Are throwaway self-deprecating bakery jokes like these allowed as personality, or do they count as adding something new to the Dorinverse? Does it matter whether a detail implies a sale (a cash register) when his bakery fills boxes for the Supper?

problem: Line 5 reads 'He will freely pardon (Isa 55:6-7). FREELY. Same price tag as the water!' This treats 'freely' in Isaiah 55:7 as 'free of charge' and ties the pardon to the water offered 'without money and without cost' in Isaiah 55:1. The BSB's 'freely' can be read as 'free of cost', but it can also mean 'generously' or 'abundantly', and the text never links the pardon in 55:7 to the price of the water in 55:1. The docs say to leave open how two things connect and that what he notices must be true, but they don't say whether a play on one English word's double meaning counts as connecting two things.
question: Can Papa Dorin play on the BSB's 'freely pardon' (Isa 55:7) as 'free of cost' and link it to the 'without cost' water of Isaiah 55:1 ('Same price tag as the water!'), or should the line keep 'freely' without tying it to the price in 55:1?

problem: The meaning of "witness" (also on stop 1 card 9) ends with "Here, David shows the nations who God is." That second sentence explains what the passage means, not what the word means. Isaiah 55:4 only says David was made "a witness to the nations", and the only source listed is Webster's Dictionary (1828), which does not say this about David. definitions.md says to summarize the source's meaning and to write each meaning for its own word, but it does not say whether a meaning may add a reading of the passage that no listed source gives.
question: May a definition add a sentence that applies the word to the passage (here, saying what David's being a witness means) when no listed source gives that reading, or should meanings stay with the word's sense from the source?

problem: The question reads "The LORD says something of His works the same way. What is it?" This is hard to parse: "works" can be read as a noun (His works) or a verb (something of His that works the same way). The intended meaning is that something of His, His word (Isaiah 55:11), does not return without doing what it was sent for. None of the cited rules is clearly broken, but the wording may confuse the baker.
question: Should the docs require choice-card questions to be clear and grammatical, and should this card be reworded, for example to "In the same way, what does the LORD say will not return to Him empty?"

problem: The blank is the next words of the same line in Isaiah 55:1 ("without money and without cost"). Card 1 quoted the first half of the verse, and this card asks the baker to fill in the rest of the wording. "Cost" adds no meaning beyond "without money", so the card tests the verse's wording, not something the baker can reason out. This is a prophetic passage.

rule.text: In poetry, letters and prophecy, the rule against guessing the next words of a line (see below) applies to fill in the blank too. The blank tests meaning the baker can reason out, not wording they haven't seen.

problem: Stop 2 card 1 says "the voice shifts" (Isaiah 55:6-7 speaks of the LORD in the third person). Card 4 then quotes a first-person line ("For My thoughts are not your thoughts...") and only names the speaker at the end, through the BSB's "declares the LORD". Right after a voice shift, the baker reads "My" without knowing who is speaking. The card should say the LORD is speaking before the quote starts.

rule.text: When he quotes someone speaking as "I," he says who it is first.

problem: The question opens "In this joyful picture", which points back to story cards the baker can no longer see. Calling it "joyful" also gives the answer away, because thornbushes and briers spreading is plainly not joyful, so the setup rules out the wrong answer.

rule.text: The story card before it isn't on screen anymore, so the question says who and what. Never "him," "that" or "it" pointing back to a card the baker can't see.

problem: Two jokes have Papa Dorin sulking: "Somebody calls my stamps crooked and I sulk for a week" (1/10 Rejoice) and "if somebody skipped the thank you on one cookie, I'd be sulking by the oven for an hour" (2/10 ungrateful). In the same lesson he says "I don't hold grudges, friend" (2/12 forgiven). papa-dorin.md wants self-deprecating humor but also says he never holds a grudge and his humor reflects kindness and forgiveness.
question: Is self-deprecating humor about sulking or staying upset fine for Papa Dorin, or does it clash with "He never holds a grudge"?

problem: Some right-answer explanations open with praise that works like a reaction: "False, and nice catch!" (1/13), "False, and you caught it!" (3/16), "You got it." (1/6), "That's the one, friend." (2/4), "That's it, baker." (3/18). The code already shows a right-answer reaction first. These phrases aren't in the reaction list, so the rule doesn't clearly cover them.
question: Does "The explanation never includes a reaction" mean only the listed reaction phrases, or any praise opener like "nice catch!" and "You got it"?

problem: The "You brood of vipers" explanation says "Those words come from John the Baptist, friend" (Luke 3:7). That's true in Luke, but Jesus Himself says "brood of vipers" in Matthew 12:34 and 23:33. A baker who knows Matthew may read this as saying Jesus never used the phrase.
question: When a wrong answer points to another passage, should Papa Dorin stick to the same book (here Luke), or must the claim hold for the whole Bible?

problem: The "old" explanation says "The question is true or false." On a fill-in-the-blank card this reads as if the card were a true/false question. It means the contrast is true versus false prophets, but the passage never says "true prophets" (Luke 6:23 just says "the prophets"). The "false" explanation also calls them "the real prophets."
question: Is this wordplay clear enough, and is "real/true prophets" an acceptable way to name "the prophets" of Luke 6:23?

problem: Both explanations turn the text's "will be like his teacher" (Luke 6:40) into resemblance in appearance: True says "Fully trained means looking like the one who trained you" and follows with a joke about how his early stamps "looked like a smudge"; False says the student "ends up looking like the one who did the training." The verse says the trained disciple will be like his teacher, not that he will look like him. Keep the text's wording ("be like").

rule.text: Call things what the text calls them.

problem: The "You brood of vipers" explanation says "Those words come from John the Baptist, friend" (Luke 3:7). John does say them in Luke 3:7, but Jesus also says "brood of vipers" in Matthew 12:34 and Matthew 23:33. Papa Dorin knows the whole Bible, so presenting the phrase as John's alone is not fully true. A wording like "In Luke, those words come from John the Baptist" would keep it accurate.

rule.text: Noticing. What he points out must be true.

problem: Several self-deprecating lines present new habits or reasons as facts about Papa Dorin rather than as hypotheticals: "Somebody calls my stamps crooked and I sulk for a week" (stop 1, card 10, right answer), "I get nervous lending out my good apron" (stop 2, card 2, "Your belt as well"), and "I don't hold grudges, baker, and this line is a big reason why" (stop 2, card 12, "forgiven"), which gives his no-grudge trait a new reason not in his backstory. The docs encourage self-deprecating humor ("He's happy to be the joke") but also say he "never adds anything new" to his backstory and that he is "Always positive" and "never holds a grudge." Hypotheticals like "if somebody cursed at me, my mustache would be tied in a knot" seem clearly fine. The docs do not say where the line is.
question: Can Papa Dorin's jokes state present-tense habits or feelings about himself (sulking for a week over criticism, being nervous to lend his apron), or give new reasons for his traits ("this line is a big reason why" he doesn't hold grudges)? Or must such lines stay hypothetical ("if...") so they add nothing new to the Dorinverse and don't sit against his positive, no-grudge character?

problem: The Big Idea leaves out the opening scene in Luke 6:17-19: Jesus comes down to a level place, a huge crowd comes from Judea, Jerusalem, Tyre and Sidon to hear Him and be healed, and power comes from Him and heals them all. Line 1 opens with 'here's the whole sermon in one box' and goes straight to the Beatitudes.
question: In a Sermons passage, does 'covers the whole passage' mean the Big Idea must also mention the setting verses before the sermon starts (here the healings in Luke 6:17-19), or is covering the sermon itself enough?

problem: The Big Idea leaves out the opening of the passage completely. In Luke 6:17-19 the crowds come from Judea, Jerusalem, Tyre and Sidon to hear Jesus and be healed, and power comes from Him and heals them all. The rest of the Big Idea covers the sermon itself (Luke 6:20-49).
question: In a Sermons passage, does "It covers the whole passage" mean the Big Idea must also mention the story around the sermon (here the crowd and the healings in Luke 6:17-19), or is it enough to cover the sermon?

problem: Line 6 drops the "like" from Jesus' comparison. The BSB says the one who hears and acts "is like a man building a house, who dug down deep and laid his foundation on the rock" (Luke 6:47-48). Line 6 says the one who hears and acts "builds on the rock, and when the torrent hits, that house doesn't shake." That turns the comparison into a plain statement about what the hearer does. It should keep the comparison, for example: that person is like a man who built his house on the rock.

rule.text: Keep "like," "as," "if" and "though" as they are.

problem: Line 1 lists the poor, the hungry and the weeping (Luke 6:20-21) and the woes (Luke 6:24-26), then says "What you've got NOW isn't the whole story, because 'great is your reward in heaven' (Luke 6:23)." In the BSB, the reward in heaven in Luke 6:23 goes with those who are hated, excluded and insulted "because of the Son of Man" (Luke 6:22). That group isn't mentioned at all. The poor, hungry and weeping each get their own promise (the kingdom of God, being filled, laughing). Line 1 ties the 6:23 reward to groups the text doesn't tie it to.

rule.text: Leave open what the text leaves open. Who is being spoken to, why, or how two things connect.

problem: The Big Idea still leaves out the opening of the passage. In Luke 6:17-19 Jesus comes down to a level place, crowds come from Judea, Jerusalem, Tyre and Sidon to hear Him and be healed, and power comes from Him and heals them all. Line 1 starts with "here's the whole sermon in one box" and goes straight to Luke 6:20.
question: In a Sermons passage, does "It covers the whole passage" mean the Big Idea must also mention the setting before the sermon starts (here the crowd and the healings in Luke 6:17-19), or is covering the sermon enough?

problem: Stop 1, card 18 says "bless those who curse them" (Luke 6:28). "curse" gets a pop-up on this card, but "bless" does not. The only related entry is "blessed", which means "Truly happy and well off because God shows them His favor." That fits Luke 6:20-22, but not the verb in Luke 6:28, where blessing someone means wishing good on them or asking God to do them good. So the opposite of the defined word "curse" on the same card has no pop-up, and the "blessed" meaning would not help here. definitions.md says "A word always has the same meaning, so each word appears once", but it does not say what to do when a related form of a defined word ("bless" next to "blessed") has a different sense in the passage.
question: Should "bless" on stop 1, card 18 get its own entry with the sense used in Luke 6:28, separate from "blessed"? Or should related forms with a different sense be left out?

problem: This passage is a Sermon. The 'Poetry, letters and prophecy' rules (never guess the next words of a line, fewer choice cards, blanks test meaning not wording) are written only for those three types. Many of the fill-in-the-blank cards here test exact sermon wording: Stop 1 cards 8, 15 and 17; Stop 2 cards 10, 12 and 15; Stop 3 cards 11 and 13. In stops 1 and 2, choice cards also match or outnumber story cards, as they would in a story.
question: Should Sermon passages (teaching with little narrative) follow the poetry/letters/prophecy rules on guessing wording and using fewer choice cards, or the normal story rules?

problem: The rule 'An included parable or sermon (see passages.md) gets a stop of its own' doesn't say what to do when the whole passage is a sermon. Here the narrative setting (Luke 6:17-19) shares Stop 1 with the start of the sermon, and the sermon is split across three stops. passages.md was not provided to check against.
question: When the passage type is Sermons, may the sermon be split across several stops, and should the narrative setting before it get its own stop or share one?

problem: The passage type is Sermons. The poetry, letters and prophecy rules (never guess the next words of a line, fill in the blank tests meaning not wording, fewer choice cards, up to 4 story cards in a row) don't say whether they cover sermons. Many choice cards here test exact wording of Jesus' lines: stop 1 cards 8 (laugh), 15 (false prophets) and 17 (enemies), stop 2 cards 10 (ungrateful), 12 (judged and forgiven) and 15 (measure), and stop 3 cards 11 (fruit) and 13 (mouth).
question: Should Sermons passages follow the poetry, letters and prophecy rules, so that fill in the blank and other choice cards don't ask the baker to supply Jesus' exact wording? If they should, these cards need to be reworked.

problem: The opening card gives context from the passage before (Jesus has just chosen His twelve apostles up on the mountain, Luke 6:12-16) but cites only Luke 6:17. The docs say the opening card gives context and that the passage before is context only, not part of the lesson. They don't say whether an opening card can state facts from that passage, or how to cite them.
question: Can the opening card state facts from the passage before as context? If it can, should it cite those verses (here Luke 6:12-17), or keep the reference inside the lesson's passage?

problem: The 'verses' field on a choice card is both what the card cites and the verses of the right answer. When a question retells an earlier verse for context (stop 1 cards 2 and 10, and the 'level place' detail from Luke 6:17 in stop 1 card 4), the card's reference and the right answer's reference are different, but there is only one field.
question: When a choice card's question retells earlier verses for context, should 'verses' cover everything the card uses or only the right answer's verses? Should the schema get a separate field for the answer?

problem: The card puts quotation marks around "Blessed." with a period inside, but in the BSB (Luke 6:20) the word runs straight on: "Blessed are you who are poor...". The quoted punctuation isn't the BSB's. Card 6's question has the same "Blessed." quote. Either drop the period or quote more of the line exactly.

rule.text: Quotation marks around Bible words mean the exact BSB wording, punctuation included.

problem: "One more woe. Woe to you when all men speak well of you." only restates the verse. It has none of Papa Dorin's voice: no reaction, no comparison, no storyteller line.

rule.text: Short, but not stripped down. A story card still has enough of Papa Dorin's voice and enough context that the moment makes sense.

problem: "Then Jesus says: 'Be merciful, just as your Father is merciful.'" is only the verse with a lead-in. Papa Dorin's voice is missing.

rule.text: Short, but not stripped down. A story card still has enough of Papa Dorin's voice and enough context that the moment makes sense.

problem: "Then Jesus says a disciple is not above his teacher." is a bare paraphrase of half of Luke 6:40, with none of Papa Dorin's voice.

rule.text: Short, but not stripped down. A story card still has enough of Papa Dorin's voice and enough context that the moment makes sense.

problem: The right answer, "A good measure pressed down and running over", uses the passage's own distinctive wording. It sounds more like the Bible than the plain wrong answers ("A small portion carefully counted out", "A little left over from the harvest"), so it stands out. The wrong answers are also clearly stingy, which goes against the generous giving Jesus has just described.

rule.text: Don't let the right answer stand out. All the answers should sound alike. None should sound more like the Bible, or more modern, than the others.

problem: This passage's type is Sermons. The walkthrough's special handling covers only "Poetry, letters and prophecy": no guessing the next words of a line (including fill in the blank), fewer choice cards, and up to 4 story cards in a row. Sermons aren't mentioned there. This Prep treats the sermon like a narrative, and several fill-in-the-blank cards ask the baker to supply Jesus' exact next word. Examples: stop 1 card 15 ("the ___ prophets" / false), stop 2 card 10 ("kind to the ___ and wicked" / ungrateful), stop 2 card 15 ("with the ___ you use" / measure) and stop 3 card 13 ("the ___ speaks" / mouth). Some can be reasoned out, but they test wording.
question: Should Sermons passages follow the Poetry, letters and prophecy rules (no guessing the next words of a line, fewer choice cards, 4 story cards in a row allowed), or the narrative rules as this Prep does?

problem: The opening card says "Jesus has just chosen His twelve apostles up on the mountain". That fact comes from the passage before (Luke 6:12-16), but the card cites only Luke 6:17. The docs let the opening card give context when the passage starts mid-thought. They also say every fact comes from the passage text and that each card cites exactly the verses it uses. They don't say how context from the preceding passage should be cited, or whether it may be stated as fact at all.
question: When the opening card uses context from the preceding passage, should it cite those verses (for example Luke 6:12-17), cite only the lesson passage, or avoid stating prior-passage facts?

problem: More than 3 New Testament commands qualify, and Prep asked a choice card about at least seven of them: Luke 6:27 (1/17), Luke 6:28 (1/18), Luke 6:29 (2/2), Luke 6:31 (2/4), Luke 6:35 (2/8), Luke 6:37 (2/12), Luke 6:42 (3/9).
